summary: Specifies how to use the Triple-DES encryption algorithm in cipher feedback mode with the Telnet encryption option.

eli5.summary: This picks one particular scrambling method, Triple-DES, for hiding Telnet text.

subtitle: How to protect a Telnet session with Triple-DES in cipher feedback mode, using 64-bit blocks.

tldr.problem: The Telnet encryption option needs concrete ciphers, each with its own type code, setup commands and key rules.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines Triple-DES in cipher feedback mode as encryption type 3. The sender announces a random 8-byte initial vector, the receiver accepts it, and keys are cut from the authentication key.
tldr.outcome: It gives confidentiality but not integrity: an active attacker has a limited ability to modify predictable text, which the RFC accepts to avoid the cost of a MAC on slow links.

facts.label: Initial vector
facts.value: 8 bytes (64 bits), sent in clear text

facts.label: Keys derived
facts.value: Up to 6 DES keys of 8 bytes

today: RFC 2947 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2000, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It has a sibling, RFC 2948, which defines the output feedback variant.

sections.title: Triple-DES in Cipher Feedback Mode for Telnet
sections.content:
RFC 2947 plugs one more cipher into the Telnet encryption option. It defines how to use Triple-DES (the data encryption standard applied three times) in cipher feedback mode, with 64-bit chunks, to protect a Telnet session.

The document does not describe Telnet encryption as a whole. It only fills in the pieces a cipher must supply: a type code, a few suboption commands for exchanging an initial vector, the rules for restarting the cipher, the algorithm itself and the way to build keys from an authentication exchange.
sections.eli5: Telnet already has a way to say "let's scramble our chat". This document picks one scrambling recipe, Triple-DES, and writes down exactly how to use it.

sections.title: Command Names and Meanings
sections.content:
The cipher is encryption type DES3_CFB64, code 3. Three suboption commands carry the initial vector (IV) setup: CFB64_IV (1), CFB64_IV_OK (2) and CFB64_IV_BAD (3).

The side that is WILL ENCRYPT generates a random 8-byte initial vector and sends it in clear text with CFB64_IV. Only that side may send this command. The side that is DO ENCRYPT answers with CFB64_IV_OK or CFB64_IV_BAD, and only that side may send those replies.

CFB64_IV_OK MUST be sent, for backwards compatibility with existing implementations. The RFC sees no reason to send CFB64_IV_BAD except after a protocol violation, such as an IV that is not 8 bytes long.
sections.eli5: One side picks a random starting number and tells the other side. The other side says "got it" so both can start scrambling the same way.

sections.title: Starting, Stopping and Restarting Encryption
sections.content:
Once CFB64_IV_OK has been received, the WILL ENCRYPT side should negotiate a key identifier (keyid) with the ENC_KEYID command. When a common keyid is found, that side may send START and END commands, and data is then encrypted with the DES3 64 bit Cipher Feedback algorithm.

The RFC then lists when the encryption (decryption) machine must be re-initialized:

  • If encryption is turned off and on again with the same keyid, the clear text in between must not change the state of the machine.
  • A START with a different keyid re-initializes it right after the command, using the new key and the IV from the last CFB64_IV.
  • A new CFB64_IV while encryption is enabled re-initializes it right after the command, using the new IV and the keyid from the last START.
  • A CFB64_IV while encryption is not enabled waits: the machine is re-initialized after the next START, with that command's keyid and this IV.
sections.eli5: Whenever the key or the starting number changes, both sides reset their scrambler at the same moment. If they did not, they would stop understanding each other.

sections.title: The Algorithm
sections.content:
The cipher works on 64-bit (8-byte) chunks. iV is the 64-bit initial vector, Dn is the nth chunk of data to encrypt (decrypt) and On is the nth chunk of output. One Triple-DES step is DES encrypt with key1, DES decrypt with key2, then DES encrypt with key3.

V0 = DES-e(DES-d(DES-e(iV, key1),key2),key3)
On = Dn ^ Vn
V(n+1) = DES-e(DES-d(DES-e(On, key1),key2),key3)

The key point of cipher feedback is the last line: the next block of keystream is made by running the previous output chunk On through the Triple-DES step. The output is XORed with the input data.
sections.eli5: The scrambler makes a secret strip of numbers and mixes it into your message. Each new piece of the strip is made from the scrambled message so far.

sections.title: Getting Keys from Telnet Authentication
sections.content:
A keyid of zero means the default encryption key, such as one derived from the Telnet AUTHENTICATION option. If that default key has fewer than 16 bytes, DES3_CFB64 must not be offered or used.

The available key data is cut into 8-byte DES keys, labeled key1 through key6 (key1 is the first 8 bytes, and so on). How many keys there are decides which keys the server and the client use for their encrypt, decrypt, encrypt steps. Server-to-client data always uses the pattern shown for the server, and client-to-server data uses the client pattern. In all cases the keys must have their parity corrected after they are chosen.

The RFC admits that this assumes it is safe to use a non-DES key, or part of one, as a DES key. That is not true of every cipher system, but it is the default because it holds for most authentication systems in use and keeps compatibility with existing implementations. New AUTHENTICATION mechanisms may define their own key derivation if their session key is not a DES key.
sections.eli5: The secret from logging in is chopped into pieces, and the pieces are handed out as keys. The server and the client use them in different orders, so each direction has its own lock.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Cipher Feedback encryption does not ensure data integrity. An active attacker who can predict the clear text has a limited ability to modify it. The limits are real: only 8 bytes can be changed at a time, and the following 8-byte block is corrupted, which makes detection likely. Still, the RFC says an active attacker might exploit the weakness.

The trade-off is performance. Adding a message authentication code (MAC) would greatly increase the bytes needed to send a single character over Telnet, which hurts slow (dialup) links.
sections.eli5: The scrambling hides the message but does not stop someone from tampering with it. A tamper-proof seal would make every little message much bigger, which is slow on slow connections.
